# On the Strange Grace of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking a lot lately about the moments that don't matter. Not the big ones—not graduations or proposals or the day you get that job or lose that person. Those moments get written down, photographed, remembered with intent. I'm talking about the other ones. The ones that slip past like water through your fingers, leaving no trace except maybe a faint impression that something small and good happened.

I was at a coffee shop yesterday—one of those indie places with mismatched furniture and a barista who actually knows people's names—and I watched a woman read a book. That's it. Nothing happened. But she was so completely absorbed in whatever world she was visiting that her coffee went cold beside her. Every few minutes she'd unconsciously tuck a strand of hair behind her ear in the same exact way, a gesture so habitual it seemed to come from some deeper part of her than consciousness. She made tiny facial expressions—a slight smile at something, a small frown of concern for her fictional character. She was living two lives at once, present in the coffee shop and completely elsewhere, and there was something beautiful about that duality that I can't quite articulate.

This is what I mean about ordinary moments. They're everywhere. They're invisible. They're the actual substance of life, and yet we've been culturally trained to ignore them, to wait for the important moments, to live life as a series of checkpoints rather than as an ongoing experience.

I think this has something to do with narrative. We're all obsessed with stories—we consume them constantly, in every form available to us—and stories have arcs. They have beginnings and middles and ends. They have climaxes. A story about someone reading a coffee shop for twenty minutes doesn't have an arc. It just is. And because it just is, with no narrative tension or resolution, we dismiss it as unimportant. But if ordinary moments aren't important, what is? What's the alternative?

The alternative seems to be constant dissatisfaction. Always waiting for the good part. Always thinking, "Well, this is fine, but just wait until..." And then you die and you realize you spent the whole time waiting.

I don't want to be melodramatic about it. I'm not going to say that every moment is precious, because I don't think that's true. Some moments are genuinely dull. Some are painful. Some are just filler, and it would be lying to pretend otherwise. But there are so many moments—more than we can possibly count or remember—that are actually quite nice if we pay attention to them.

My neighbor has a dog, a ridiculous-looking thing with legs too short for its body and an expression of permanent bewilderment. Every morning I hear it attempting to bark, which sounds more like a squeaky toy than an actual bark, and then I hear my neighbor apologizing to someone for the noise. There's something endearing about that. There's a whole relationship implied there—between my neighbor and the dog, between my neighbor and the apologized-to stranger. Lives intersecting and separating, the dog contributing something utterly unintended but somehow exactly right to the morning soundscape of the neighborhood. If I start thinking about the dog too much, I smile. I can't help it.

What am I doing, smiling at the thought of a neighbor's dog? Nothing. Nothing at all. And yet something too.

I think we've made a fundamental error in how we understand meaning. We've decided that meaning comes from outcomes. That something is meaningful if it results in achievement or recognition or change. But what about the meaning that comes from simple appreciation? From noticing? What if meaning is something more like attention itself—the act of really looking at a thing, rather than through it?

There's a Buddhist concept I like, though I'm sure I'm not explaining it properly since I only have a tourist's knowledge of Buddhism. The idea that you should do everything with complete presence and intention, whether you're meditating or washing dishes or having a conversation. That the quality of attention you bring to a task is what matters, not the task itself. This extends to observation too. The quality of your attention to a moment determines the quality of that moment's existence in your mind. Two people can experience the exact same thing, and one person walks away enriched while the other walks away unchanged. The difference is attention.

This is something I'm still learning, or relearning maybe, because I think children are naturally good at this before we train it out of them. I watched my young cousin watch an ant for fifteen minutes the other day. Not for any purpose. She wasn't trying to learn about ants or complete some educational task. She just became curious about this one ant and followed it around the yard, completely engaged. She narrated what it was doing as if announcing a nature documentary: "Now the ant is climbing. Now the ant has found a leaf. Now the ant is lifting the leaf." It was the most important thing in the world to her at that moment, and that attention made it genuinely interesting, even for me, even though I was watching her watch an ant rather than watching the ant itself.

Somewhere between childhood and now, we get trained out of that kind of attention. We learn that there are important things to pay attention to and unimportant things, and we should really focus our energy on the important category. Which makes logical sense, I suppose. If we paid rapt attention to everything, we'd be paralyzed. But the result is that we zoom through our lives, checking boxes, waiting for the things that are worth our attention according to the metrics we've internalized.

And then we wake up and years have gone by.

I want to be clear that I'm not anti-achievement or anti-goals. I think those things matter too. I think wanting to build something or accomplish something or become better at something is completely valid and important. But I don't think those things should be the only things we value, and I don't think they should be the basis for whether a day felt good or was worthwhile.

Some of the best days of my life involved no achievement whatsoever. There was a day recently when I did absolutely nothing, and I mean nothing—no productivity, no exercise, no self-improvement, no checking off tasks. I sat around in old clothes, read a book that wasn't going to make me smarter, talked to a friend for hours without any particular purpose, ate food that was probably not great for me, and watched the light change in my apartment as the day progressed. By every measure of success I've been taught, it was a completely wasted day. And yet it was one of those days where I went to sleep feeling like I had actually lived, rather than just existed while thinking about living.

Why is there a guilt associated with those days?

I think it's because we're all operating on a default setting of scarcity mindset. The idea that time is a finite resource we must allocate carefully, that every hour spent on something that doesn't "count" toward some larger goal is an hour wasted. And yes, time is finite. We all have a limited amount of it. But it seems to me that the way most of us spend our finite time—always reaching toward some future state where finally we'll have enough time or money or success to relax and actually enjoy things—is a strange kind of waste too. We're burning the only time we definitely have in service of some future moment of peace we might never reach.

I'm not saying to quit your job and abandon your responsibilities. I'm just saying that I think we could all afford to be a bit gentler with ourselves about the value of simply existing. About the moments that don't produce anything but a memory, and often not even that—just a feeling that something was okay.

There's a word in Japanese, "ma," that refers to negative space or the emptiness between things. It's not considered empty at all in the traditional sense—it's seen as essential, full of potential, meaningful in itself. I think that's what I'm trying to get at. The space between achievements, the gaps between important moments, the ordinary stretches of life that seem empty but are actually where most of the substance is.

One more example: my mother and I made cookies yesterday. It was pointless in the sense that we could have bought cookies, better cookies, from literally anywhere. We made them from scratch and they came out slightly burnt on the edges and not as evenly shaped as they should have been. But we stood in her kitchen and she told me a story about my grandfather that I'd never heard before—something about him trying to fix something mechanical and getting so frustrated he kicked it, and then being embarrassed about his own temper. It was such a small story. It doesn't change anything. But something about standing there with our hands covered in flour, laughing about my grandfather's long-dead frustration while cookies baked, felt important in a way that success and failure don't quite capture.

That's the thing about ordinary moments. They often only reveal their value in retrospect. You don't know while you're in them that they're going to mean something. You just find out later, sometimes much later, when you remember something small and it brings you comfort or joy or a sense of connection.

I think that's okay. I think we can stop demanding that every moment justify itself in real time. We can stop asking "Is this worth my time?" about everything and instead just experience things and see what sticks.

I'm sitting here finishing this piece and I'm not sure I've really made a coherent point. I've mostly just tried to articulate a feeling, that there's something valuable in the space between important moments, something that gets lost when we structure our lives entirely around achievements and goals. I think the best life would be one where you pursued meaningful goals and built things and tried to grow, but also where you made space for those moments that don't count for anything. The coffee shop reading. The squeak of the neighbor's dog. The afternoon that produces no output. The conversation that goes nowhere. The simple presence of existing alongside other people, doing nothing in particular.

Maybe that's what grace is—the unexpected kindness of a moment you didn't even know to expect. The ordinary made luminous, not through any effort of your own, but just through paying attention.
